b20-anskey.title: The missing answer key (Medium)
b20-anskey.html:
The missing answer key

A quiz had five true/false questions, Q1 to Q5. Five students answered every question; their answers are shown below (T = true, F = false). Each correct answer earned 1 mark and there was no negative marking. The answer key has been lost.

StudentQ1Q2Q3Q4Q5

ChitraFTTTF

  • Asha, Chitra and Esha got the same score.
  • Each of Asha, Chitra and Esha scored more than Bharat.
  • Dev scored less than every other student.

b20-siblings.title: Five siblings (Easy)
b20-siblings.html:
Five siblings

Anil, Babita, Chirag, Dimple and Ekta are siblings. Their ages are whole numbers of years, and no two of them are the same age.

  • Their ages add up to 50 years.
  • Anil is 4 years older than Chirag.
  • Babita is twice as old as Dimple.
  • Ekta is 3 years older than Anil.
  • Dimple is older than Chirag.
  • Babita is the eldest, and she is 8 years older than the youngest sibling.

b20-parcels.title: Parcels weighed in pairs (Medium)
b20-parcels.html:
Parcels weighed in pairs

Five parcels P, Q, R, S and T have different weights, each a whole number of kilograms, with P < Q < R < S < T. Every one of the ten possible pairs of parcels was put on a scale together, and the ten readings were written down without noting which pair gave which reading. The readings, in kg, in increasing order were:

11, 13, 16, 17, 20, 20, 22, 23, 25, 29

b20-rps.title: Rock, paper, scissors (Hard)
b20-rps.html:
Rock, paper, scissors

Ravi and Sima played 9 rounds of rock–paper–scissors. In each round both show one hand at the same time: rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper and paper beats rock; the same hand on both sides is a draw.

  • None of the 9 rounds was a draw.
  • Ravi showed rock 4 times, paper 3 times and scissors 2 times.
  • Sima showed rock 2 times, paper 3 times and scissors 4 times.
  • Sima won more rounds than Ravi.
  • Ravi won at least two rounds.

b20-pebbles.title: Passing pebbles (Medium)
b20-pebbles.html:
Passing pebbles

Four children, A, B, C and D, start a game with 11, 7, 4 and 2 pebbles respectively. The game is played in rounds. In each round, the child holding the most pebbles gives one pebble to each of the other three children. If two or more children are tied for the most, the one who comes first in alphabetical order gives.

b20-auction.title: Sealed-bid auction (Medium)
b20-auction.html:
Sealed-bid auction

Four collectors, W, X, Y and Z, each start with 100 tokens. Five lots are auctioned one after another, Lot 1 to Lot 5. Before the auction each collector wrote down a planned bid for every lot (table below). The rules are:

  • For each lot, a collector's actual bid is the planned bid, or the tokens he has left at that moment if that is smaller.
  • The highest actual bid wins the lot, but the winner pays the second-highest actual bid for that lot.
  • If two collectors tie for the highest bid, the one with more tokens left wins (this never happens below).

b20-exams.title: Exam timetable (Medium)
b20-exams.html:
Exam timetable

Six papers — Accounts, Biology, Chemistry, Drawing, Economics and French — are to be held over eight days, Day 1 to Day 8, at most one paper a day. So exactly two days have no paper (free days).

  • There is a paper on Day 1 and on Day 8, and the two free days are not next to each other.
  • Biology is held before Chemistry, and they are not on consecutive days.
  • Economics is held exactly three days after Accounts, and there is no free day between them.
  • French is held on the day just after a free day.
  • Biology is held on an even-numbered day.
  • Chemistry is held after French.

questions.question: How many of the five questions have the answer 'true'?
questions.solution: Asha and Chitra differ only on Q1 and Q3, so equal scores mean the key matches Asha on exactly one of them: the key has the same value for Q1 and Q3. Asha and Esha differ only on Q3 and Q4, so in the same way the key has the same value for Q3 and Q4. Hence Q1 = Q3 = Q4 in the key. Let x (0, 1 or 2) be the number of the questions Q2, Q5 on which the key matches Asha's answers (T, F). If Q1 = Q3 = Q4 = F: Asha = 1 + x and Dev = 2 + (2 − x) = 4 − x (Dev's Q2, Q5 answers are the opposite of Asha's). Dev below Asha needs x = 2, but then Bharat = 1 + 0 = 1 is below Dev's 2, so Dev is not the lowest — this case fails. If Q1 = Q3 = Q4 = T: Asha = 2 + x, Chitra = 2 + x, Esha = 2 + x, Bharat = 2 + (2 − x) = 4 − x and Dev = 1 + (2 − x) = 3 − x. Asha > Bharat needs 2 + x > 4 − x, so x = 2: Q2 = T and Q5 = F. Key: T, T, T, T, F. Scores: Asha 4, Bharat 2, Chitra 4, Dev 1, Esha 4, and Dev is lowest ✓. A computer check of all 32 possible keys finds only this one. The key has 4 trues.

questions.question: How old is Dimple (in years)?
questions.solution: Let Chirag be c and Dimple d. Then Anil = c + 4, Ekta = c + 7 and Babita = 2d, so the total is 3c + 3d + 11 = 50, giving c + d = 13 with d > c. The youngest is Chirag (Anil and Ekta are older than Chirag, and so are Dimple and Babita), so 2d − c = 8. With c + d = 13 this gives 3d = 21: d = 7, c = 6. Ages: Anil 10, Babita 14, Chirag 6, Dimple 7, Ekta 13 (total 50 ✓, Babita eldest ✓).

questions.question: Who is the second eldest of the five?
questions.solution: Let Chirag be c and Dimple d. Then Anil = c + 4, Ekta = c + 7 and Babita = 2d, so the total is 3c + 3d + 11 = 50, giving c + d = 13 with d > c. The youngest is Chirag (Anil and Ekta are older than Chirag, and so are Dimple and Babita), so 2d − c = 8. With c + d = 13 this gives 3d = 21: d = 7, c = 6. Ages: Anil 10, Babita 14, Chirag 6, Dimple 7, Ekta 13 (total 50 ✓, Babita eldest ✓). In order of age: Babita 14, Ekta 13, Anil 10, Dimple 7, Chirag 6.

questions.question: After how many years will the combined age of Chirag and Dimple equal Babita's age at that time?
questions.solution: Let Chirag be c and Dimple d. Then Anil = c + 4, Ekta = c + 7 and Babita = 2d, so the total is 3c + 3d + 11 = 50, giving c + d = 13 with d > c. The youngest is Chirag (Anil and Ekta are older than Chirag, and so are Dimple and Babita), so 2d − c = 8. With c + d = 13 this gives 3d = 21: d = 7, c = 6. Ages: Anil 10, Babita 14, Chirag 6, Dimple 7, Ekta 13 (total 50 ✓, Babita eldest ✓). After t years: (6 + t) + (7 + t) = 14 + t, so 13 + 2t = 14 + t and t = 1.

questions.question: What is the total weight (in kg) of all five parcels?
questions.solution: Each parcel appears in 4 of the 10 pairs, so the readings add up to 4 × (total weight): 196 = 4 × total, total = 49 kg. The two lightest readings must be P + Q = 11 and P + R = 13; the two heaviest must be S + T = 29 and R + T = 25. Then R = 49 − (P + Q) − (S + T) = 49 − 11 − 29 = 9, so P = 13 − 9 = 4, Q = 7, T = 25 − 9 = 16 and S = 13. Check: the ten sums of 4, 7, 9, 13, 16 are exactly 11, 13, 16, 17, 20, 20, 22, 23, 25, 29 ✓ (a computer search over all sets of five weights up to 40 kg finds no other).

questions.question: How many rounds did Ravi win?
questions.solution: Write RP for 'Ravi rock, Sima paper' and so on; with no draws there are six kinds of round. Let RP = x. Ravi's rocks: RP + RS = 4, so RS = 4 − x. Sima's paper: RP + SP = 3, so SP = 3 − x. Ravi's scissors: SR + SP = 2, so SR = x − 1. Sima's rock: PR + SR = 2, so PR = 3 − x. Ravi's paper: PR + PS = 3, so PS = x. (Sima's scissors: RS + PS = 4 ✓.) So 1 ≤ x ≤ 3. Ravi wins with RS, PR and SP: (4 − x) + (3 − x) + (3 − x) = 10 − 3x; Sima wins the other 3x − 1. x = 1 gives Ravi 7 wins (Sima does not win more); x = 3 gives Ravi only 1 win; so x = 2. Rounds: RP 2, RS 2, PR 1, PS 2, SR 1, SP 1. Ravi won 4 rounds and Sima 5.

questions.question: In how many rounds did Ravi's rock lose to Sima's paper?
questions.solution: Write RP for 'Ravi rock, Sima paper' and so on; with no draws there are six kinds of round. Let RP = x. Ravi's rocks: RP + RS = 4, so RS = 4 − x. Sima's paper: RP + SP = 3, so SP = 3 − x. Ravi's scissors: SR + SP = 2, so SR = x − 1. Sima's rock: PR + SR = 2, so PR = 3 − x. Ravi's paper: PR + PS = 3, so PS = x. (Sima's scissors: RS + PS = 4 ✓.) So 1 ≤ x ≤ 3. Ravi wins with RS, PR and SP: (4 − x) + (3 − x) + (3 − x) = 10 − 3x; Sima wins the other 3x − 1. x = 1 gives Ravi 7 wins (Sima does not win more); x = 3 gives Ravi only 1 win; so x = 2. Rounds: RP 2, RS 2, PR 1, PS 2, SR 1, SP 1. Ravi won 4 rounds and Sima 5. RP = x = 2.

questions.question: In how many rounds did Ravi show paper and win?
questions.solution: Write RP for 'Ravi rock, Sima paper' and so on; with no draws there are six kinds of round. Let RP = x. Ravi's rocks: RP + RS = 4, so RS = 4 − x. Sima's paper: RP + SP = 3, so SP = 3 − x. Ravi's scissors: SR + SP = 2, so SR = x − 1. Sima's rock: PR + SR = 2, so PR = 3 − x. Ravi's paper: PR + PS = 3, so PS = x. (Sima's scissors: RS + PS = 4 ✓.) So 1 ≤ x ≤ 3. Ravi wins with RS, PR and SP: (4 − x) + (3 − x) + (3 − x) = 10 − 3x; Sima wins the other 3x − 1. x = 1 gives Ravi 7 wins (Sima does not win more); x = 3 gives Ravi only 1 win; so x = 2. Rounds: RP 2, RS 2, PR 1, PS 2, SR 1, SP 1. Ravi won 4 rounds and Sima 5. Ravi's paper wins against rock: PR = 1.

questions.question: If the last condition (Ravi won at least two rounds) were dropped, how many different values would be possible for the number of rounds Ravi won?
questions.solution: Write RP for 'Ravi rock, Sima paper' and so on; with no draws there are six kinds of round. Let RP = x. Ravi's rocks: RP + RS = 4, so RS = 4 − x. Sima's paper: RP + SP = 3, so SP = 3 − x. Ravi's scissors: SR + SP = 2, so SR = x − 1. Sima's rock: PR + SR = 2, so PR = 3 − x. Ravi's paper: PR + PS = 3, so PS = x. (Sima's scissors: RS + PS = 4 ✓.) So 1 ≤ x ≤ 3. Ravi wins with RS, PR and SP: (4 − x) + (3 − x) + (3 − x) = 10 − 3x; Sima wins the other 3x − 1. x = 1 gives Ravi 7 wins (Sima does not win more); x = 3 gives Ravi only 1 win; so x = 2. Rounds: RP 2, RS 2, PR 1, PS 2, SR 1, SP 1. Ravi won 4 rounds and Sima 5. Without that condition both x = 2 and x = 3 are allowed, giving Ravi 4 or 1 wins — two possible values.

questions.question: Who gives pebbles in round 3?
questions.solution: Holdings (A, B, C, D) after each round: start (11, 7, 4, 2); round 1, A gives: (8, 8, 5, 3); round 2, A gives (tie with B, A first): (5, 9, 6, 4); round 3, B gives: (6, 6, 7, 5); round 4, C gives: (7, 7, 4, 6); round 5, A gives: (4, 8, 5, 7); round 6, B gives: (5, 5, 6, 8); round 7, D gives: (6, 6, 7, 5) — the same as after round 3. So from round 3 on the holdings repeat every 4 rounds, with givers C, A, B, D in rounds 4, 5, 6, 7, then 8, 9, 10, 11, and so on.

questions.question: How many pebbles does D hold after round 50?
questions.solution: Holdings (A, B, C, D) after each round: start (11, 7, 4, 2); round 1, A gives: (8, 8, 5, 3); round 2, A gives (tie with B, A first): (5, 9, 6, 4); round 3, B gives: (6, 6, 7, 5); round 4, C gives: (7, 7, 4, 6); round 5, A gives: (4, 8, 5, 7); round 6, B gives: (5, 5, 6, 8); round 7, D gives: (6, 6, 7, 5) — the same as after round 3. So from round 3 on the holdings repeat every 4 rounds, with givers C, A, B, D in rounds 4, 5, 6, 7, then 8, 9, 10, 11, and so on. After round r (r ≥ 3) the holdings depend on r mod 4: 50 leaves remainder 2, the same as round 6, so D holds 8.

questions.question: In how many of the first 20 rounds is A the child who gives?
questions.solution: Holdings (A, B, C, D) after each round: start (11, 7, 4, 2); round 1, A gives: (8, 8, 5, 3); round 2, A gives (tie with B, A first): (5, 9, 6, 4); round 3, B gives: (6, 6, 7, 5); round 4, C gives: (7, 7, 4, 6); round 5, A gives: (4, 8, 5, 7); round 6, B gives: (5, 5, 6, 8); round 7, D gives: (6, 6, 7, 5) — the same as after round 3. So from round 3 on the holdings repeat every 4 rounds, with givers C, A, B, D in rounds 4, 5, 6, 7, then 8, 9, 10, 11, and so on. A gives in rounds 1, 2, 5, 9, 13 and 17 — 6 times.

questions.question: Over the first 100 rounds, what is the smallest number of pebbles held by any child at the end of a round?
questions.solution: Holdings (A, B, C, D) after each round: start (11, 7, 4, 2); round 1, A gives: (8, 8, 5, 3); round 2, A gives (tie with B, A first): (5, 9, 6, 4); round 3, B gives: (6, 6, 7, 5); round 4, C gives: (7, 7, 4, 6); round 5, A gives: (4, 8, 5, 7); round 6, B gives: (5, 5, 6, 8); round 7, D gives: (6, 6, 7, 5) — the same as after round 3. So from round 3 on the holdings repeat every 4 rounds, with givers C, A, B, D in rounds 4, 5, 6, 7, then 8, 9, 10, 11, and so on. D has 3 after round 1; after that every state in the cycle has at least 4 in each hand (round 2's smallest is 4 too). So the minimum is 3.

questions.question: How many tokens does Z have left at the end of the auction?
questions.solution: Lot 1: Z bids 45 (highest), second-highest is W's 40 — Z pays 40 and has 60 left. Lot 2: X 45 wins and pays Y's 40 (X left 60). Lot 3: Y 45 wins and pays W's 35 (Y left 65). Lot 4: Z 45 (Z still has 60) wins and pays X's 40 — Z has 20 left. Lot 5: Z's planned 40 is cut to 20 tokens; W 50 wins and pays the second-highest actual bid, X's 30 (W left 70). Final tokens: W 70, X 60, Y 65, Z 20.

questions.question: Which lot was sold for the lowest price?
questions.solution: Lot 1: Z bids 45 (highest), second-highest is W's 40 — Z pays 40 and has 60 left. Lot 2: X 45 wins and pays Y's 40 (X left 60). Lot 3: Y 45 wins and pays W's 35 (Y left 65). Lot 4: Z 45 (Z still has 60) wins and pays X's 40 — Z has 20 left. Lot 5: Z's planned 40 is cut to 20 tokens; W 50 wins and pays the second-highest actual bid, X's 30 (W left 70). Final tokens: W 70, X 60, Y 65, Z 20. Prices: 40, 40, 35, 40, 30 — Lot 5 at 30 is the lowest.

questions.question: If bids were never cut down to the tokens a collector has left (everything else unchanged), how many tokens would W have at the end?
questions.solution: Lot 1: Z bids 45 (highest), second-highest is W's 40 — Z pays 40 and has 60 left. Lot 2: X 45 wins and pays Y's 40 (X left 60). Lot 3: Y 45 wins and pays W's 35 (Y left 65). Lot 4: Z 45 (Z still has 60) wins and pays X's 40 — Z has 20 left. Lot 5: Z's planned 40 is cut to 20 tokens; W 50 wins and pays the second-highest actual bid, X's 30 (W left 70). Final tokens: W 70, X 60, Y 65, Z 20. Only Lot 5 changes: Z's bid stays 40, so W still wins with 50 but pays 40 instead of 30, ending with 100 − 40 = 60.

questions.question: If instead the winner of each lot paid his own actual bid (everything else unchanged), how many tokens would Z have at the end?
questions.solution: Lot 1: Z bids 45 (highest), second-highest is W's 40 — Z pays 40 and has 60 left. Lot 2: X 45 wins and pays Y's 40 (X left 60). Lot 3: Y 45 wins and pays W's 35 (Y left 65). Lot 4: Z 45 (Z still has 60) wins and pays X's 40 — Z has 20 left. Lot 5: Z's planned 40 is cut to 20 tokens; W 50 wins and pays the second-highest actual bid, X's 30 (W left 70). Final tokens: W 70, X 60, Y 65, Z 20. With pay-your-bid: Z wins Lot 1 for 45 (55 left), X wins Lot 2 for 45, Y wins Lot 3 for 45, Z wins Lot 4 for 45 (10 left), and W wins Lot 5 for 50 (Z's bid is cut to 10). Z ends with 10.

questions.question: With as many workers as needed, what is the minimum number of days to finish the whole renovation?
questions.solution: With enough workers, every task starts as soon as its predecessors finish. Finish days: A 3, B 4, C 5, D 9 (after A and B), E 8, F 13 (after D at 9 and E at 8), G 6, H 11. So the project needs 13 days, along the chain B → D → F (4 + 5 + 4). Working backwards from day 13, the latest finishes are A 4, B 4, C 6, D 9, E 9, F 13, G 8, H 13, so the slacks are A 1, B 0, C 1, D 0, E 1, F 0, G 2, H 2.

questions.question: With as many workers as needed and the renovation finishing in the minimum time, which tasks can each be delayed by 2 days without delaying the finish?
questions.solution: With enough workers, every task starts as soon as its predecessors finish. Finish days: A 3, B 4, C 5, D 9 (after A and B), E 8, F 13 (after D at 9 and E at 8), G 6, H 11. So the project needs 13 days, along the chain B → D → F (4 + 5 + 4). Working backwards from day 13, the latest finishes are A 4, B 4, C 6, D 9, E 9, F 13, G 8, H 13, so the slacks are A 1, B 0, C 1, D 0, E 1, F 0, G 2, H 2. Only G and H have a slack of 2 days.

questions.question: If only two workers are available, what is the minimum number of days needed?
questions.solution: With enough workers, every task starts as soon as its predecessors finish. Finish days: A 3, B 4, C 5, D 9 (after A and B), E 8, F 13 (after D at 9 and E at 8), G 6, H 11.
